newsitem.title: INDIA: Dalai Lama pins hopes on "gentle" Jiang over Tibet.
newsitem.headline: Dalai Lama pins hopes on "gentle" Jiang over Tibet.

text.p: Exiled Tibetan leader the Dalai Lama said China's new supreme leader Jiang Zemin could help resolve the Tibetan issue positively.

"Judging during the Tiananmen event, when he was mayor of Shanghai...he handled the demonstrations quite gently, and in a positive way. And that is an indication," the Dalai Lama told Reuters Television at his Indian headquarters in Dharamsala.

But Tibet's spiritual leader, who fled to India in 1959 after a failed anti-Chinese uprising in his homeland, said China's communist system could still thwart any efforts by Jiang to settle Tibet's status, even if he decided to make them.

"As for the totalitarian system which is constitutionalised with Marxist ideology, (with) one or two persons, it is difficult to change the system... But I always believe change will come," he said on Saturday.

The Dalai Lama paid tribute to Jiang's mentor, the late Deng Xiaoping, but said the former Chinese patriarch was a man of few words. "Of course he was one of the great new revolutionaries, and also I think in certain fields very diplomatic, and in certain fields very stubborn," the Dalai Lama said of the man he last met in Beijing in 1955.
"I want to mention that in 1979, my elder brother, my personal emissary, had a long meeting with (Deng)," the Dalai Lama said.
"At that time he stated that (except) the question of Tibetan independence, anything can be discussed regarding Tibetan issues.

"You see this problem is neither good for China or for Tibet -- so we have to find a solution to this problem (and I had) very much hoped that within his lifetime we could find a mutually agreeable solution.
"But that did not happen, and that is my regret," the Dalai Lama said.
Tibet was ruled by a theocratic Buddhist elite until 1950 when China's People's Liberation Army took over the area.
The Dalai Lama's remarks on Deng were at variance with the views of a government-in-exile he heads in Dharamsala.
A statement by the government which no country recognises accused Deng on Thursday of being "directly responsible for decades of repression and suffering in Tibet".

"No living Chinese leader today may have as much personal interest in retaining China's stranglehold on Tibet as did Deng," the statement from the Central Tibetan Administration in Dharasala, in the northern Himalayan foothills, said.

It said Deng was personally involved in China's major campaigns against Tibet, and cited the invasion of the region, communist reforms, the crushing of the 1959 uprising and the suppression of independence demonstrations.
"Therefore any admission of China's failures in Tibet would have amounted to a personal loss of face and reputation for Deng," it said.
In 1988, the Dalai Lama tempered his calls for Tibetan independence by proposing a five-point plan for autonomy which would let China control Tibet's foreign affairs.

"We hope that Deng's successor, Jiang Zemin, will find courage to solve the Tibetan problem in the spirit of tolerance, reconciliation and compromise," the government-in-exile said, referring to Deng's anointed heir and Communist Party chief.
